title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Ever since Levin had first looked into the questions of life and death by his beloved brother's deathbed — in the light of what he called these new convictions, which between the ages of twenty and thirty-four had quietly taken the place of his boyhood and youthful beliefs — he had been gripped by a horror, not so much of death as of life: a life with no knowledge of where it came from, why, how, or what it was. The physical organism, its decay, the indestructibility of matter, the law of conservation of energy, evolution — these were the words that had pushed his old faith out of the way. The words and the ideas attached to them were perfectly serviceable for intellectual work. But for life itself they offered nothing, and Levin felt suddenly like a man who has traded a warm fur cloak for a thin muslin shirt and, going out into the frost for the first time, is convinced — not by reasoning but by his whole body — that he is as good as naked and certain to perish horribly.
From that moment on, even though he didn't put it to himself directly and went on living as he always had, Levin had never lost that sense of terror at how little he knew.

He also dimly felt that what he called his new convictions weren't merely a gap in his knowledge — they were part of a whole framework of ideas inside which the knowledge he needed simply wasn't available.

At first, marriage, with all the new joys and responsibilities that came with it, had crowded these thoughts out completely. But lately — while he was staying in Moscow after his wife's confinement, with nothing in particular to do — the question that demanded an answer had been pressing on him more and more often, more and more insistently.

He boiled it down to this: "If I don't accept the answers Christianity gives to the basic problems of my life, what answers do I accept?" And in the whole stockpile of his convictions, not only did he find no satisfying answer — he could find nothing that even resembled an answer.
He was in the position of a man hunting for food in toy shops and tool shops.
Instinctively, almost unconsciously, with every book, every conversation, every person he came across, he was scanning for some light on these questions and a way out of them.

What baffled and unsettled him most was that the majority of the men of his age and class had, like him, swapped their old beliefs for the same new convictions, and yet saw nothing to regret in it — they were perfectly satisfied and at ease. So beyond the central question, Levin was tormented by other questions too. Were these people sincere? he asked himself. Or were they putting on an act? Or did they understand the answers science offered to these problems in some other, clearer way than he did? And he diligently studied both their views and the books that laid out those scientific explanations.

One thing he had figured out since these questions had taken hold of him was that he had been quite wrong in thinking — based on memories of his college circle — that religion had had its day and was now practically gone. All the people closest to him who lived good lives were believers. The old prince, and Lvov, whom he liked so much, and Sergey Ivanovitch, and all the women believed; his wife believed as simply as he had believed in his earliest childhood; and ninety-nine hundredths of the Russian people — all the working people whose lives he had the deepest respect for — believed.

Another thing he had become sure of, after reading many scientific books, was that the men who shared his views had no other interpretation to offer — they gave no explanation of the questions he felt he could not live without answering, but simply ignored that those questions existed and tried instead to explain other questions he had no interest in, such as the evolution of organisms, the materialist theory of consciousness, and so on.

On top of that, during his wife's confinement, something had happened that struck him as extraordinary. He, an unbeliever, had found himself praying, and in the moment of prayer he had believed. But that moment had passed, and he couldn't make the state of mind he had been in then fit into the rest of his life.

He couldn't admit that in that moment he had known the truth and was now wrong, because as soon as he started thinking about it calmly, the whole thing fell apart. He couldn't admit that he had been mistaken back then either, because that spiritual condition was precious to him, and to call it a sign of weakness would have been to defile those moments. He was painfully at war with himself, and he was straining every spiritual muscle to find a way out of the situation.
